extracted.intended_audience: students, readers, and practitioners of literary theory and creative writers interested in dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts guidance implied by Aristotle's Poetics about composing and judging drama—emphasis on what makes tragedy effective (plot, naturalness, emotional appeal) and common anti-patterns. Useful for playwrights, critics, and students of dramatic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of plot/story
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is to be understood primarily in terms of its story/plot; the language of drama is subordinate to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page echoes the common reading that Aristotle 'reduces the drama ... to the story' — implying that when evaluating or composing tragedy, attention should center on the unity, structure, and causal coherence of the plot rather than on decorative language alone. Anti-pattern: privileging rhetorical ornament or moralizing summaries over the work's dramatic action and structural integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write from the heart / appeal to emotion (phusikôs over logikôs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle criticizes works that are written 'exclusively from the intellect' and contrasts 'logikôs' (logically) with 'phusikôs' (naturally/appropriately); good drama speaks to feeling as well as reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose dialogue and scenes that arise from characters' natural, appropriate motivations and that move the audience emotionally; avoid purely intellectual or abstract argumentation that feels forced or 'logical' in a reproachful sense. Example on the page: Sophocles makes Antigone 'speak' from the heart, an admired quality. Scoring note: works that evoke appropriate emotional engagement are preferred to those that are merely clever or logically persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid crudely moralistic reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce tragedy to simplistic moral fables; avoid readings or compositions that collapse complex tragic action into 'Aesop-fables' or childish moral summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page warns against 'insensitive readers' who subject stories to 'crudely moralistic readings' — as a guideline, preserve the ambiguity, complexity, and tragic magnitude of events rather than forcing a didactic moral lesson. Anti-patterns include flattening character motivation into moral aphorisms and judging a tragedy solely by a take-away moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the topic appropriately and naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical and creative treatment of dramatic subjects should be appropriate and natural (phusikôs) rather than artificial or merely logical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introductory commentary praises the Poetics for treating its topic 'appropriately and naturally'—as a production guideline, aim for choices (plot moves, character behavior, rhetoric) that feel true to the dramatic world and situation. This overlaps with the appeal-to-emotion criterion but emphasizes overall tonal and formal appropriateness rather than only emotional force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from close reading of exemplars (respect the classical model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study and respect exemplary predecessors (e.g., Homer); close textual attention to models informs better composition and judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The note that Aristotle 'respected Homer' and corrected a copy of the Iliad suggests a rubric of close reading and deference to strong exemplars: read and learn from masterworks, examine their structure and choices, and allow that study to inform one's own practice rather than dismissing tradition out of hand.
